lesson.title: Form Factor: Why RMS and Average Aren't the Same Number
lesson.summary: Form factor compares a waveform's RMS value to its rectified average value, exposing how much a signal's shape differs from a flat level, a distinction that matters for how meters and rectifier circuits are calibrated.
lesson.body:
RMS value and average value both try to summarize a whole waveform with a single number, but they are built from different math. Average value adds up the instantaneous values over one cycle and divides by the period, using the rectified, all positive version of an AC waveform, since a symmetric AC signal's plain average is zero. RMS value squares the instantaneous values first, averages the squares, then takes the square root, which weights large excursions more heavily than small ones. Because squaring emphasizes the peaks more than a simple average does, RMS is always at least as large as the average for a given waveform. Form Factor is defined as Form Factor = RMS Value divided by Average Value, and it measures exactly how much that squaring operation inflates the effective value relative to the plain average.

For a sine wave with peak value Vp, the RMS value is 0.707 times Vp, and the rectified average value is 2 divided by pi times Vp, which works out to 0.6366 times Vp. Dividing gives Form Factor = 0.707 divided by 0.6366 = 1.11. For a concrete case, take a 100 V peak sine wave: RMS is 70.7 V, rectified average is 63.7 V, and 70.7 divided by 63.7 confirms a form factor of 1.11, the classic textbook value for a sine wave.

Now contrast that with a symmetric square wave that swings between plus and minus Vp. Its instantaneous magnitude is always exactly Vp, so its RMS value, its peak value, and its rectified average value are all equal to Vp. Its form factor is Vp divided by Vp, which is 1, the smallest a form factor can be, reflecting the fact that a square wave delivers its full peak value at every instant with no wasted dips the way a sine wave has near its zero crossings.

Form factor is not just a curiosity. Many inexpensive analog meters, and simple rectifier based measurement circuits, measure the rectified average of a signal because that is mechanically or electronically easy to do, then multiply by a fixed scale factor of 1.11 to display an RMS reading, on the assumption that the signal is a clean sine wave. If you feed such a meter a square wave, a triangle wave, or distorted AC power, all of which have different form factors, the 1.11 correction is wrong and the displayed reading is inaccurate, which is exactly why true RMS meters exist as a more expensive but more general alternative.
